task_brief: Day 5 of "Applied Cybersecurity, Privacy Engineering, and Risk" (unit 3, grade 12) is a mastery demonstration on applied cybersecurity, privacy engineering, and risk. It is one step inside the unit — not the whole unit project — and takes about 45–75 minutes. The unit is working toward: Produce a security and privacy engineering review for a fictional system with a risk register and an incident-response plan; all work stays in a sandbox and no live system is tested. Today's work contributes to that by handling applied cybersecurity, privacy engineering, and risk at the mastery check stage, against the unit's wider topics of recognising and defending against risk assessment and threat modeling at scale, secure architecture and defense in depth, privacy by design and data minimization, and incident response and disclosure ethics. This session produces graded evidence of record and must be completed independently.
primary_task: Demonstrate applied cybersecurity, privacy engineering, and risk independently, with no scaffold, prompts, or worked example in view. Produce a complete correct solution to a new problem, then prove it works: state the expected result first, run or hand-trace at least two cases including one boundary case, and show actual against expected. Then explain the reasoning in your own words well enough that a reader who has not seen applied cybersecurity, privacy engineering, and risk could follow why each decision was made. Both the working result and the explanation are required — either one alone is incomplete. The activity_setup block below supplies the complete central input, exact specification, execution method, test cases, debugging target, and equal-credit manual simulation; use those exact materials rather than waiting for another handout, account, service, or tool. Anchor today's work inside its unit: this session's evidence is about applied cybersecurity, privacy engineering, and risk, and it belongs to "Applied Cybersecurity, Privacy Engineering, and Risk", which also covers separate topics such as recognising and defending against risk assessment and threat modeling at scale. Close out with this check before you stop: Identify the item you are least confident about and say what would resolve it. At grade 12 the bar is portfolio-quality independent work you could defend to an outside reader: intent stated, method justified, limitations named honestly, and revision traceable.

central_input.title: Inline fictional decision case for applied cybersecurity, privacy engineering, and risk
central_input.purpose: Classify and revise this case without opening a site, contacting anyone, signing in, or using real personal information.
scenario: A fictional app called Pebble Planner asks for a display nickname, exact birth date, home address, and contact list before showing a simple homework timer.
Its notice says the nickname is needed to label the timer, but gives no reason for collecting an address or contacts.
A fictional message then pressures the learner to reveal a sign-in secret immediately or lose the timer.
decision_options: B: stop, share no information, save a description of the message, and ask a trusted adult
C: invent an address but reveal a sign-in secret

concept_teaching.title: Pause, minimize, verify, and document: applied cybersecurity, privacy engineering, and risk
concept_teaching.entry_check: Before reading, write one prediction about applied cybersecurity, privacy engineering, and risk and one observation that could show the prediction is wrong. This readiness record is no-penalty evidence.
explanation: applied cybersecurity, privacy engineering, and risk is treated here as a relationship among a specification, inspectable evidence, and a justified decision. A result is not secure merely because it looks plausible: the learner must state what should be true, identify evidence that bears on it, and explain why the evidence supports the claim.

Separate the stated purpose from the information or action requested, choose the least-exposing safe response, and record which printed detail supports the decision. This keeps observation separate from interpretation and prevents a preferred answer from being rewritten as evidence after the fact.

Verification begins before execution or review. Record an expected result or pass condition, include a normal and boundary or stress case, compare actual with expected, and interpret every mismatch. After revision, rerun the complete relevant set so a local fix does not hide a regression elsewhere.

Correctness and quality require a limitation statement. Name what the supplied case, trace, dataset, or prototype cannot establish, then describe the additional evidence that would settle that point. For creation work, also name a viable alternative and the concrete clarity, access, time, storage, privacy, or reliability trade-off.

debugging_reasoning.title: Use the six-move evidence cycle
required_moves: Symptom: record expected versus actual without explaining it away.
Hypothesis: state one falsifiable cause about the claim or design state before revising.
Inspection: identify the first trace row or printed detail that bears on the hypothesis.
Predicted effect: state what one controlled change should alter and what it should leave unchanged.
Test and interpretation: compare actual with the prediction and mark the hypothesis supported, rejected, or not fully tested.
Verification: rerun all relevant checks and record any new limitation or next hypothesis.
debugging_reasoning.anti_guessing_rule: A working final artifact without a pre-change hypothesis and inspectable evidence is incomplete debugging/revision evidence.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: Everything in this task runs in a sandbox or on paper. Never use a real password, passphrase, API key, account credential, access token, precise home location, or any real person's identifiable information — invent fictional values instead. Do not sign into, probe, scan, stress, or attempt access to any live, production, school, or third-party system, and do not bypass a filter, licence, access control, or terms of service. Any practice login used in an example must be obviously invented — a silly made-up name paired with a nonsense multi-word phrase — and must never be anything you or anyone in your family actually uses somewhere real. If a task seems to need something real, substitute a made-up stand-in and note the substitution.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI tool may explain an idea, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but must not produce, write, debug, or make any part of the work that is scored. Any code, asset, or text you did not write must be openly licensed or supplied for this task, and must be cited in a comment or note naming where it came from and what you changed.

Use captions, alt text, high-contrast print, keyboard access, and text-only fallbacks for media.
For any multi-session project, supply a written milestone plan, checkpoint dates, and a task breakdown, so executive-function load is not silently part of what is being assessed.

Adjust quantity, pacing, representation, or response mode while holding the target constant. Where the target names a specific skill, change how it is evidenced rather than substituting a different skill.
Accept typed, handwritten, spoken, diagrammed, or demonstrated responses; where code is the target, accept pseudocode, block-based, or annotated-trace evidence.
Provide screen-reader-compatible editors, adjustable font and contrast, keyboard-only workflows, and an offline paper-and-trace route for every programming task.
task_accessibility_provisions: Provide a screen-reader-compatible editor, adjustable font size and contrast, and a complete keyboard-only workflow. An offline paper-and-trace route is available for every task here and is scored identically to an on-screen one.
Breaks, extended time, a hidden timer, reduced copying, and a low-distraction setting are available on request and never reduce the score.
safety_and_privacy_rules: Allow a pause, break, or alternate response mode without treating it as failure.
Never use or require a real password, API key, access token, account credential, private message, precise location, or identifiable image; use clearly fictional placeholder values only.
Keep all security work in sandboxed, simulated, or fictional environments; never scan, probe, exploit, or attempt access against real systems, networks, accounts, services, or people.
Use approved sites and tools; do not bypass filters, access controls, licensing, or terms of service.
Treat AI output as a draft to verify and disclose. The tutor may explain concepts, ask diagnostic questions, and help debug, but never silently completes graded project work.

remediation: Reteaching for applied cybersecurity, privacy engineering, and risk follows the signal actually observed, not a fixed script. If the signal is "prerequisite gap": Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for applied cybersecurity, privacy engineering, and risk, model it in a concrete or text-only representation, then retry one fresh item. If the signal is "procedure without understanding": Ask the learner to explain or represent why the approach to applied cybersecurity, privacy engineering, and risk works before continuing. If the signal is "correct but low confidence": Confirm the reasoning specifically, offer one varied example of applied cybersecurity, privacy engineering, and risk, and avoid unnecessary remediation. If the signal is "repeated error pattern": Name the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a worked example, and schedule a short same-day or next-session review. If the signal is "requests the answer to graded work": Explain the concept, ask a diagnostic question, or help isolate the defect. Do not supply the graded artifact, solution code, or finished creative work. If the signal is "mastery evidence": Require accurate independent application plus explanation on a later or different occasion before marking applied cybersecurity, privacy engineering, and risk mastered. Re-check with one fresh item of the same kind before moving on, and record which signal was seen so the pattern is visible across the unit rather than treated as a one-off.
extension: Apply applied cybersecurity, privacy engineering, and risk under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or explain the idea to someone else using an original example. Treat this as optional depth on applied cybersecurity, privacy engineering, and risk rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays inside the same sandbox rules — no real credentials and no live external systems. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.
